h1: Wine tourism as a second income for a winery
title: Wine Tourism as a Second Income | Craft Beer School
desc: How wineries earn from visitors: tours, tastings, food, events and stays, with the costs, licences and limits to check first.
teaser: Visitors can add a second income to a winery, but only if the place is worth the journey and the rules allow it.
standfirst: Wine tourism turns a winery into a destination. Here is what it can add, what it costs and how to test the idea before spending on it.
sections:
Wine tourism is any paid visit to a winery or vineyard: a tour, a tasting, a meal, an event, a harvest experience or a stay. It can add income beyond bottles and bring people who then buy wine, join a club and tell friends.

It also changes the business. A winery that welcomes visitors is part farm, part factory and part hospitality venue. Each part needs different skills.

People come for a place, a story and an experience: seeing vines, tasting with the maker, eating good food or relaxing in a pleasant setting. They rarely come only for a lecture on winemaking. Think about what a family, a couple or a group of friends would enjoy for half a day.

Be honest about your site. A winery with a view and a short drive from a city has an easier job than one on a hard road with no shade. Talk to travel operators and local hotels to see who would send guests.

Think about the first five minutes. Where do guests park, who greets them, where do they wait and is there shade? Clear signs, clean toilets and drinking water do more for reviews than a clever tasting menu. Offer non-alcoholic choices and seating for those who do not drink, since groups include drivers and non-drinkers.

• Tastings and tours, usually the first offer.
  • Food: a cafe, a picnic or a pairing menu.
  • Events such as harvest days, dinners and private parties.
  • Accommodation, which is a separate hospitality business.
  • Retail: bottles, glasses and local products.

Each stream has its own margin and licence needs. Add them one at a time. A winery that opens a restaurant, rooms and an event lawn at once can lose focus and cash.

Events deserve care. A private dinner or celebration brings a large single payment but needs staff, noise limits and rules on late service. Agree capacity, hours and clean-up with the hosts in writing. Harvest experiences, where guests pick or sort fruit, are popular, but they come at the busiest and hottest time for your team, so charge accordingly and brief guests on safety.

Hospitality adds rules: food safety, fire and building safety, parking, toilets, insurance and alcohol licences. Rules on tastings, on-site sales and events differ by country and, in India, by state. They also change. Check with the regulator, the local authority and a licensing adviser before you promise anything to a guest.

Responsible service matters. Check age and offer water and food. Help guests find safe transport home.

Insurance is easy to forget. Public liability cover for visitors on a working site is a basic need. Ask an insurer who understands farms and hospitality what they would require.

Use a simple model. Visitors per week times share who buy times average spend gives sales. Subtract staff, food costs, utilities and wear on the site. As an illustration with made-up numbers: 200 visitors a week at an average spend of 40 units gives 8,000 units. If staff and costs take 6,000, the margin is thin. Adding a higher-margin experience or lifting average spend by a few units improves it without adding staff. More visitors usually bring more staff cost with them.

Seasons matter. Many places have a busy period and a quiet one. Plan staff and cash for both. See running a tasting room as a business.

Start small: weekend tastings, a booking system, a few staff. Count visitors and spend for a season. If the numbers work, add the next stream. If they do not, you have lost little. Use feedback to improve the visit and to refine what you sell in the shop.

Wine tourism supports the wider plan. A tourist who tries your wine may become a club member. See wine clubs for small wineries.

Record who comes, how they heard of you, what they bought and what they said. Ten honest comments teach more than a marketing plan. Use them to decide which stream to add next.
faqs: Do I need a restaurant for wine tourism?
No. Many wineries start with tastings and simple food. They add more only if the numbers support it.
What licences does wine tourism need?
Alcohol, food, fire and building approvals vary by country and Indian state. Ask the regulator and local authority.
It can be, but staff, food and upkeep take a share. Model it from your own figures.
Partner with local hotels, tour operators and event planners. Keep a clear website with hours and prices.
